tier_reason: First-party blog comparing v0.5.0 (Tokio, readiness/epoll-based) with v0.7.0 (compio thread-per-core io_uring). The linked dashboard reports (benchmarks.iggy.apache.org/api/benchmark/full/<uuid>) give the CPU (Intel Xeon Platinum 8259CL, AWS i3en.3xlarge), OS, kernel and exact iggy-bench commands, and the bench code is public in apache/iggy core/bench. Rust compiler version and build flags are stated nowhere, so it cannot be A, and being first-party it is not B.

corrections.workload: iggy-bench pinned-producer over TCP, 1000-byte messages, 250 msgs/batch: 8x8 (20 GB), 16x16 (40 GB) and 32 producers x 32 streams (80 GB / 80M msgs) at a 1 GB/s rate limit, plus unthrottled fsync (strong consistency) runs at 16 and 32 partitions; compares Iggy v0.5.0 (Tokio) with v0.7.0 (thread-per-core io_uring via compio)
corrections.hardware: AWS i3en.3xlarge: Intel Xeon Platinum 8259CL @ 2.50GHz, 12 cores, ~93 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.17.0-1007-aws (from the linked benchmarks.iggy.apache.org report JSON)
corrections.caveats: First-party engineering blog; hardware/OS/kernel/bench commands confirmed through the dashboard report API, but the Rust toolchain and build flags are unstated. The baseline is Iggy's own earlier Tokio build (epoll readiness model), not a standalone epoll loop. Latency is compared at a fixed 1 GB/s rate limit, so throughput is equal by construction outside the fsync runs. At 8 producers, P95/P99 are slightly worse on v0.7.0 (-8%/-3%); the gains grow with partition count.

notes: All claimed numbers match the blog's 32x32 and fsync-32 tables exactly. The benchmark dashboard's JSON API (/api/benchmark/full/<uuid>) exposes hardware and params that the JS-rendered UI hid. The linked reports also include some 0.6.1-edge.4 runs.

tier_reason: First-party README JMH tables against Java FileChannel, with public bench code at src/test/java/bench/random (read/ and write/). Hardware is only 'a Linux machine', and the JDK version and JVM flags are unstated, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Reads, 25 threads, registered files vs pre-opened FileChannel: +55% at 512B (29,023 vs 18,769 ops/ms), +489% at 4KB (13,393 vs 2,275), +23% at 16KB, +16% at 64KB; open/read/close +13% to +48%; blocking + virtual threads +14% to +138%. Writes, single thread: +123% to +246% (4KB 860 vs 260 ops/ms, +231%); 8 threads +33% to +77% but -3% at 64KB; 20 threads 0% (512B), -2% (4KB), -16% (16KB), -33% (64KB), so FileChannel wins high-concurrency writes.
corrections.caveats: First-party README benchmark; no CPU model, JDK version or JVM flags stated (only 'a Linux machine', JMH, 2,211 ops/invocation, QD 256, random offsets). The headline 489% uses io_uring registered files vs pre-opened FileChannels at 25 threads. Writes lose to FileChannel at 20 threads by up to 33% (64KB). Unlicense is a public-domain dedication: no patent grant.

notes: The headline numbers (489%, 231%, 860 vs 260) are exact, but the record's 'reverses slightly (-2%) at 20+ threads' understates the write regression: the README shows -16% at 16KB and -33% at 64KB at 20 threads. So claimed_speedup was corrected and the verdict is downgrade, with the tier still C. baseline_in_list=false is correct: FileChannel is not among the event-loops-io baselines.
